evidence.title: Angkor Wat, Angkor Thom, Roluos & Banteay Srei (Siem Reap, Cambodia): Khmer Temple-Mountain Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Sanskrit-Khmer steles, LiDAR urban grid & hydraulic barays
evidence.summary: Spanning over 400 sq km of baray reservoirs and carved temple-mountains culminating in Suryavarman II's Angkor Wat and Jayavarman VII's Bayon–Ta Prohm monastic universities, Angkor stood as the preindustrial world's largest low-density sacred agro-urban metropolis.
evidence.limits: Airborne LiDAR reveals immense surrounding wooden suburbs long invisible beneath jungle canopy.

evidence.title: Sambor Prei Kuk / Ishanapura (Kampong Thom, Cambodia): 7th-c. Pre-Angkorian Chenla Brick Sanctuaries
evidence.dateBasis: King Isanavarman I Sanskrit inscriptions & octagonal brick towers
evidence.summary: Preceding Angkor by two centuries along the Sen River, Chenla's capital of Ishanapura preserves dozens of octagonal brick sanctuaries decorated with carved 'flying palace' reliefs — the cradle of classical Khmer temple art and epigraphy.
evidence.limits: Secular timber neighborhoods between temple enclosures await fuller excavation.

evidence.title: Preah Vihear Cliff Sanctuary & Koh Ker Step-Pyramid Capital (Northern Cambodia): 9th–12th c. Khmer Highlands
evidence.dateBasis: Inscribed causeway pavilions & 921–944 CE Koh Ker royal steles
evidence.summary: Rising atop a sheer 525-meter Dângrêk sandstone escarpment along a 800-meter axial staircase, Preah Vihear dedicated its mountain-crown sanctuaries to Shiva beside nearby Koh Ker's 36-meter seven-tiered brick-and-laterite Prasat Thom pyramid capital.
evidence.limits: Borderland topography shaped staggered centuries of Yasovarman I to Suryavarman II construction.

evidence.title: Banteay Chhmar & Preah Khan of Kompong Svay (NW & East Angkor): Provincial Monastic Megacomplexes
evidence.dateBasis: Jayavarman VII Bayon-style lintels & baray walls
evidence.summary: Extending Jayavarman VII's Mahayana Buddhist temple-hospitals and iron-smelting hubs well beyond Siem Reap, the vast walled compounds of Banteay Chhmar and Preah Khan of Kompong Svay rivaled Angkor Thom itself in square-kilometer enclosure area.
evidence.limits: Collapse of sandstone galleries and looting impacted perimeter Lokeshvara bas-reliefs prior to stabilization.

evidence.title: Wat Phou & Champasak Sacred Mountain Temple (Southern Laos): 5th–13th c. Mekong Shiva-to-Buddha Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: 5th-c. Devanika Sanskrit stele & Khmer cliff staircases
evidence.summary: Aligned carefully between the natural linga peak of Phou Kao and the Mekong plain since the 5th century CE, Wat Phou preserves an axial stone processional staircase, spring shrine, and planned ancient riverside city Shresthapura older than Angkor.
evidence.limits: Submerged Mekong floodplains obscure portions of lower brick Shresthapura quarters.

evidence.title: Sukhothai, Si Satchanalai & Kamphaeng Phet (Thailand): 13th–15th c. Walking-Buddha Monastery Capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Ramkhamhaeng stele, Sanghalok celadon kilns & laterite wats
evidence.summary: Centered within triple earthen moats in northern central Thailand, Sukhothai and twin ceramic city Si Satchanalai built towering brick-and-laterite Mahathat stupas, Sri-Lankan-influenced Theravada *aranyavasi* forest monasteries, and glazed Sanghalok export kilns.
evidence.limits: Chronology of exact Ramkhamhaeng inscription features prompted methodological paleographic debates.

evidence.title: Ancient Town of Si Thep & Khao Klang Nok Monument (Phetchabun, Thailand): 6th–11th c. Dvaravati Urbanism
evidence.summary: Uniting twin circular moated cities in the Pa Sak valley with the massive 20-meter stepped brick stupa of Khao Klang Nok and Thamorrat cave reliefs, Si Thep links early Hindu Vishnu statues, Theravada Dvaravati Buddhist art, and later Khmer temples.
evidence.limits: Alluvial siltation obscures lower moated domestic wooden districts inside the outer rampart.

evidence.title: Prasat Phimai & Phanom Rung Sandstone Temples (Khorat Plateau, NE Thailand): Khmer Northern Road Shrines
evidence.summary: Anchored along the Royal Highway northwest out of Angkor into the Mun River valley, Phanom Rung crowns an extinct volcanic crater rim while Phimai — built largely of white sandstone as an early Mahayana prototype for Angkor Wat's lotus towers — preserves intact narrative lintels.
evidence.limits: Anastylosis reconstruction in the late 20th century reassembled fallen sandstone courses.

evidence.title: Mrauk U Stone Temple Capital (Rakhine / Arakan, Western Myanmar): 1430–1785 CE Walled Pagodas
evidence.dateBasis: Arakanese royal chronicles, Shittaung & Koe Thaung inscriptions
evidence.summary: Constructed from massive interlocked sandstone slabs wrapped through tidal river ridges between the Bay of Bengal and Arakan Yoma hills, Mrauk U's fortress-temples — led by King Min Bin's labyrinthine Shittaung ('80,000 Images', 1535) and Koe Thaung — synthesized Bengali Sultanate arches and Theravada vaulted shrines.
evidence.limits: Armed instability in Rakhine State halted full UNESCO World Heritage field nominations.

evidence.title: Shwedagon (Yangon), Thaton & Bago Shwemawdaw Mon Stupas (Lower Myanmar): Maritime Theravada Sanctuaries
evidence.dateBasis: 1485 Kalyani & Shin Sawbu Mon–Pali stone inscriptions
evidence.summary: Across the Irrawaddy–Sittaung deltas of Lower Myanmar, Mon maritime kingdoms raised the earliest gilded brick bells of Shwedagon and Bago Shwemawdaw — enlarged dramatically in the 15th century by Queen Shin Sawbu and King Dhammazedi — anchoring Theravada ordination across mainland Southeast Asia.
evidence.limits: Continuous gold-plate regilding and earth-quake rebuilds encase earliest Mon core brickworks inside modern domes.

evidence.title: Dieng Plateau (2,000 m), Candi Sewu & Ratu Boko (Central Java): 8th–9th c. Volcanic Mountain & Buddhist Shrines
evidence.dateBasis: 732–792 CE Old Javanese/Sanskrit inscriptions & andesite temples
evidence.summary: Before and alongside Prambanan, 8th-century Sanjaya kings erected Java's oldest standing Hindu stone temples amidst steam vents on the 2,000 m Dieng volcanic caldera while Sailendra builders raised Candi Sewu's 249-shrine mandala and Ratu Boko's hilltop palace complex near Yogyakarta.
evidence.limits: Mount Merapi eruptions and earthquakes toppled many outer *pervara* shrines prior to anastylosis.

evidence.title: Candi Penataran (Palatran) & Singhasari Temples (East Java): 1197–1454 CE Majapahit State Sanctuary
evidence.summary: On the slopes of Mount Kelud, Candi Penataran expanded across Kedhiri, Singhasari, and Majapahit kings into East Java's largest state temple complex — carving Ramayana and Panji reliefs in flat shadow-puppet (*wayang*) profile later shared across Bali.
evidence.limits: Wooden ceremonial halls atop stone terraced *pendopo* platforms are known from reliefs and postholes.

evidence.title: Pura Besakih (Mount Agung), Gunung Kawi & Goa Gajah (Bali): 10th–19th c. Rock-Cut Candis & Mother Temple
evidence.dateBasis: Old Balinese copperplates (882–1077 CE) & rock-cut facade inscriptions
evidence.summary: From 11th-century 7-meter memorial *candi* facades chiseled straight into volcanic river cliffs at Gunung Kawi (Pakerisan Valley) and cave sanctuaries at Goa Gajah to Pura Besakih ascending Mount Agung's slopes, Bali fused ancestral mountain worship with Hindu-Buddhist water-temple cosmology through 1900 CE.
evidence.limits: Multi-tiered thatched *meru* roofs are regularly renewed while stone bases retain classic Balinese proportions.

evidence.title: Padang Lawas / Biaro Bahal Brick Temples (North Sumatra): 10th–14th c. Tantric Esoteric Sanctuaries
evidence.dateBasis: Old Malay-Sanskrit inscriptions & Pannai brick biaro plans
evidence.summary: Scattered across dry Barisan savanna valleys of North Sumatra, over two dozen carved red-brick *biaro* temples of the Pannai polity (including Biaro Bahal I–III and Si Pamutung) preserve Tantric Vajrayana Heruka statues and fierce *kāla* reliefs along trans-Sumatran camphor-and-gold portages.
evidence.limits: Sparse absolute dates keep 10th vs. 13th-century construction sequences under stylistic refinement.

evidence.title: Po Nagar (Nha Trang) & Đồng Dương Buddhist Monastery (Champa, Central Vietnam): 8th–14th c. Brick Shrines
evidence.dateBasis: 784–875 CE Sanskrit-Cham foundation steles of Indravarman II
evidence.summary: Beside coastal Po Nagar's brick towers dedicated since 781 CE to goddess Yan Po Nagar (Mother of the Land of Champa), King Indravarman II raised at Đồng Dương (Indrapura, 875 CE) one of mainland Southeast Asia's largest brick Mahayana Buddhist monasteries.
evidence.limits: Đồng Dương's extensive brick corridors suffered severe wartime destruction leaving iconic Cham bronzes preserved in museums.

evidence.title: Yên Tử Trúc Lâm Monasteries & Temple of Literature / Văn Miếu (Northern Vietnam): 1070–1900 CE
evidence.dateBasis: 1070 Lý Thánh Tông annals, 1442–1779 doctoral steles & Yên Tử towers
evidence.summary: Extending from Hanoi's 1070 Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu, holding 82 carved stone turtle-borne doctorates, 1442–1779) eastward to cloud-wrapped Mount Yên Tử where abdicated Emperor Trần Nhân Tông founded native Trúc Lâm Zen in 1299, northern Vietnam shaped uniquely Vietnamese monastic, scholarly, and brick-stupa traditions.
evidence.limits: Subsequent Lê and Nguyễn rebuilds restored wooden pavilions over Lý–Trần stone foundations.
